content_html:
Your Percentage of a Percentage Calculator multiplies two percentages together the correct way — the way tax stacking, discount stacking, and commission-on-commission actually work — instead of the way most people guess. Enter two percentages and it gives you the combined rate instantly; add an optional starting value and it shows exactly how that value moves through both percentages, step by step.

What Does "Percentage of a Percentage" Mean?

It's what happens when one percentage applies on top of another rather than alongside it — a 40% share of something that itself represents 90% of a total, for instance. The two percentages don't describe two separate slices of the same pie; the second one describes a slice of the first one's slice.

Why You Can't Just Add Two Percentages Together

The instinct to add 40% and 90% and land on 130%, or to average them into 65%, is understandable — and wrong. Percentages that stack multiply; they don't add. A 40% cut of a 90% share isn't 130% or 65% of anything — it's 36%, because each percentage scales down whatever came before it, not the original whole.

ApproachCalculationResultCorrect?
Adding40% + 90%130%No
Averaging(40% + 90%) ÷ 265%No
Multiplying40% × 90%36%Yes

How to Calculate a Percentage of a Percentage

Here's the formula this calculator runs, laid out so you can follow — or double-check — every step by hand.

The Formula

For two percentages \(a\%\) and \(b\%\):

$$ \text{combined percentage} = \frac{a}{100} \times \frac{b}{100} \times 100 $$

Which simplifies to just multiplying the two numbers and dividing by 100:

$$ \text{combined percentage} = \frac{a \times b}{100} $$

Worked Example: 40% of 90%

  1. Convert each percentage to a decimal: 40% → 0.4, and 90% → 0.9.
  2. Multiply the two decimals: 0.4 × 0.9 = 0.36.
  3. Convert back to a percentage: 0.36 → 36%.

$$ \frac{40 \times 90}{100} = 36\% $$

So 40% of 90% is 36% — not 130%, and not 65%.

Applying the Combined Percentage to a Real Number

Percentages rarely exist for their own sake — they usually apply to an actual quantity: a price, a commission pool, a population. Enter a starting value in the calculator's optional third field and it runs both percentages against it in sequence, exactly the way a spreadsheet formula would.

Worked Example: Applying 40% Then 90% to the Value 10

StepCalculationResult
Start—10
After first percentage (40%)10 × 0.44
After second percentage (90%)4 × 0.93.6

Notice that 3.6 is also exactly what you'd get by applying the combined 36% directly to 10 in one step (10 × 0.36 = 3.6) — the two-step and one-step routes always agree, which is a good way to sanity-check either one.

Real-World Uses for Stacked Percentages

This kind of chained calculation shows up anywhere one rate is carved out of another, rather than sitting next to it.

  • Tax stacking — a local tax applied on top of a rate that already includes a state tax.
  • Discount stacking — a clearance sale's extra 20% off taken on top of an item already marked 50% off (which is not a 70% total discount — see the Percentage Off Calculator for the single-discount version of this math).
  • Commission on commission — an agent's cut of a manager's cut of a total sale.
  • Dilution — an investor's stake in a company that itself owns a percentage of another company.
  • Conversion funnels — the percentage of visitors who complete step two, out of the percentage who completed step one.
Tip: if a problem describes one percentage as being "of" or "from" another rather than simply alongside it, that's your signal to multiply the two percentages instead of adding them.

Common Mistakes

The most common error is treating stacked percentages like stacked flat amounts — adding 20% and 10% because that's how you'd combine two discounts given as dollar amounts. The second most common: stopping after converting only one percentage to a decimal and multiplying it by the other one's whole-number form (40 × 0.9 = 36, which happens to work here only because dividing by 100 once still lands on the right answer by coincidence of scale — always convert both to decimals to avoid relying on that coincidence). Keep both values in the same format, multiply, and convert back to a percentage only at the end.

faq.question: How do I calculate a percentage of a percentage?
faq.answer: Convert both percentages to decimals, multiply them together, then convert the result back to a percentage: (a% × b%) = (a × b) ÷ 100.

faq.question: Is a percentage of a percentage the same as adding two percentages?
faq.answer: No. Stacked percentages multiply, they don't add. 40% of 90% is 36%, not 130% (adding) and not 65% (averaging).

faq.question: Can the combined percentage be higher than either starting percentage?
faq.answer: No, as long as both percentages are between 0% and 100% — multiplying two proper fractions always produces a smaller fraction. It can exceed either one only if at least one input is over 100%.

faq.question: How do stacked discounts work?
faq.answer: An extra 20% off on top of an existing 50% off is not 70% total — it's applied to what's already been discounted, giving a combined discount of 60% (100% − (50% × 80% ÷ 100 × 100)).

faq.question: What is 100% of 25%?
faq.answer: 25%. Any percentage of 100% is unchanged, since 100% acts as a multiplicative identity here.

faq.question: How do I apply the combined percentage to an actual number?
faq.answer: Multiply the original value by the combined percentage as a decimal, or apply each percentage in sequence — both routes give the same answer. Enter a value in this calculator's optional third field to see both steps.

faq.question: Why isn't 40% of 90% equal to 130%?
faq.answer: Because the second percentage describes a share of the first percentage's result, not a separate amount to be added to it — the two rates compound rather than combine additively.
